name: Karl Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Karl, thanks for joining. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and what you say is confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Sunwire, a workers' co-op of twelve electricians, so I'm a part-owner as well as a spark. Most days it's solar panels, home batteries and car chargers, plus some ordinary rewiring when it's raining too hard to be on a roof. I start by asking an AI assistant to check my load calculations and draft the customer's quote while I drink my coffee in the van. The best part is showing someone their first sunny day on the app; the worst is crawling through lofts full of fibreglass in August.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Sam, who's a software tester at an insurance firm, in a rented flat near the river. I've got about ten months' costs saved plus my co-op shares, which are worth a fair bit now. We're thinking about buying next year. I'm in the union too, the co-op encourages it, and I go on climate marches more than I probably should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a useful tool, even if it's not magic. I'd post that the real revolution is batteries and heat pumps, and that's happening whatever AI does. At the co-op meeting I'd say keep using it for quotes, it saves us an hour a day each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bit disappointed, yeah. I like new toys, and I'd half hoped AI would help us run the co-op without needing an office manager. But for my actual job and money, nothing changes, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for quotes and design, and push the co-op to try a better scheduling tool. I'd put more into my co-op shares, maybe two thousand this year. And Sam and I would go ahead with buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I'm the one at Sunwire who tries every new thing first, and some of my mates tease me about it. If the big leap never comes, I'll still have my tools and my quotes done in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything on your mind for the next few years, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, mostly, because of the flat. And the solar subsidy, because if the government cut it, our order book would halve overnight. That would hurt more than any AI.

I'd post that the real revolution is **batteries and heat pumps**.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I like new toys.
I'd hoped AI would run the **co-op office** without a manager.
For my **job and money**, nothing really changes.
do: Keep using AI for **quotes** and design, and try a better **scheduling tool**.
Put **two thousand** more into my co-op shares this year.
Go ahead with **buying a flat** with Sam.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by it.

fieldNote: Karl is the **early adopter** at his co-op and uses AI daily for quotes.
His real risk in a quiet world is the **solar subsidy**, not technology.
As a **co-op owner**, he thinks about the business, not only his wage.

steps.text: Trial a new scheduling tool for the Sunwire co-op
Put two thousand more into his Sunwire co-op shares
Buy a flat with Sam next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for small firms like ours, because we can do the admin of a big firm with twelve people. I'd also say the gains should go to workers, not shareholders, and the co-op model proves it can. Online I'd be the annoying guy posting about worker ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried about Sam, not me. Testing is exactly the checking work that AI takes, and my boyfriend has already watched two people on his team not get replaced. For me, solar on roofs needs hands, and robots are slower, so I'm fine for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Sunwire using AI for the whole office side: booking, ordering, follow-up emails. We'd put the saved hours into training two more apprentices. And I'd help Sam look at moving into something more hands-on, maybe even with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Me, fine. Us, the household, a bit wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sam is a software tester. How does this land for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, I think. His firm has already frozen hiring. We've talked about him doing an electrical course, half joking, but it's not really a joke anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at Sunwire itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the AI handle quotes, stock and bookings properly, so our admin person, Nia, can move into running the battery maintenance side. The co-op means we vote on it, so nobody gets cut without a say. That's the point of owning your own firm.

say: I'd say small firms like ours can now do **big-firm admin** with twelve people.
I'd say the gains should go to **workers**, and co-ops prove it can.
think: I'm worried about **Sam**, because software testing is exactly the checking work AI takes.
Solar on roofs needs **hands**, so I'm fine for a good while.
do: Get Sunwire using AI for **booking, ordering** and follow-up emails.
Put saved hours into training **two more apprentices**.
Help Sam look at moving into **hands-on work**.
feel: **Uneasy**: I'm fine, but the **household** feels a bit wobbly.

fieldNote: Karl's risk is **household**, not personal: his partner Sam's testing job is exposed.
He would **automate the co-op office** but redeploy staff, using the co-op vote.
He sees **worker ownership** as the fair way to share AI gains.

steps.text: Set up AI booking, ordering and quoting across the Sunwire office
Use saved office hours to train two more apprentices
Help Sam look into an electrical course or co-op job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a shorter working week and public ownership of the big AI firms. I'd be at every march. At work I'd say the co-op has to move fast, because the big firms will be buying robots in 2031 and we need to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary, but not hopeless. Sam's job goes in 2028, almost for sure, and then mine is up for grabs in 2031. But we have savings, and I know these tools better than most sparks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying the flat and keep our cash. I'd get Sam into an electrical apprenticeship at Sunwire straight away, if the others vote yes. And I'd push the co-op to put money into whatever install robots arrive first, so we own them instead of competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Exciting in a strange way too, but mainly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three years before robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are everything. That's the time when hands-on work still needs us, while the office stuff goes. So the co-op would build up savings, and I'd learn the robot systems as soon as there are any to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put off, or bring forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put off the flat, definitely, because I don't want a mortgage on one wage. Bring forward Sam's career change, and bring forward my own idea of doing the master electrician's licence. I'd rather be the person who designs the system than the one who fits it.

say: I'd push for a **shorter working week** and public ownership of big AI firms.
I'd tell the co-op to **move fast** before the big firms buy robots in 2031.
think: Sam's job goes in **2028**, almost for sure, and mine is up for grabs in **2031**.
We have **savings**, and I know these tools better than most.
do: Hold off on **buying the flat** and keep our cash.
Get Sam into an **apprenticeship** at Sunwire if the co-op agrees.
Push the co-op to **buy install robots** so we own them.
S2.quote: I'd push the co-op to put money into whatever install robots arrive first, so we own them instead of competing with them.
fieldNote: Karl expects a **household earner** to lose his job in 2028, which makes him anxious despite savings.
His answer to robots is **ownership**: the co-op buying them, not fighting them.
He'd move toward **design work** with a master electrician's licence.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and keep the deposit in cash
Propose a Sunwire apprenticeship for Sam at the next co-op vote
Push Sunwire to buy the first install robots on the market
Start the master electrician's licence this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance, so let's not waste it like we wasted the warnings on climate. I'd want a law that AI firms pay a levy into retraining. And I'd tell everyone in the co-op network to start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the middle ground. Robots by 2034, I'm thirty-five, and the co-op has time to adjust. I'd treat it as a project, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat after all, maybe a smaller one. I'd do my master's licence in the next two years and start learning robot install systems as soon as manufacturers offer courses. And Sam would retrain properly, not in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also quite energised. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. He could do a proper two-year course instead of grabbing whatever's open. He's been saying he'd like to do energy-efficiency surveys, which suits him because he's a details person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still march?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. I'd march for the levy and for the shorter week. I'm the guy who brings the homemade banner.

I'd want a **levy** on AI firms paying for retraining.
think: Robots by **2034** gives the co-op time to adjust.
I'd treat it as a **project**, not a disaster.
do: Do my **master's licence** in two years, then learn robot install systems.
Help Sam **retrain properly** as an energy-efficiency surveyor.
S3.quote: Five years is a chance, so let's not waste it like we wasted the warnings on climate.
fieldNote: The extra years turn Karl's fear into **planning energy**.

steps.text: Buy a smaller flat with Sam on two incomes
Finish the master electrician's licence within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version, and we should use the time to make it fair. I'd post about building worker co-ops now, so the people who do the work own the robots later. People would roll their eyes, but that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots is plenty of time for me. I'd be forty, probably running the co-op's design side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'd do anyway. Buy the flat, do the master's licence, keep using AI every day. I'd push Sunwire to set up a training fund for members, a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe complacency. Ten years is long enough that people forget, and then it's suddenly 2035 and nobody's ready. I'd set a reminder for myself every year to check where things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sunwire look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd love Sunwire to be twenty members owning a few install robots, with people like me doing the design and testing. Fewer of us on roofs in August, which I wouldn't miss. That would be the dream.

say: I'd say this is the **best version**, so use the time to make it **fair**.
I'd post about building **worker co-ops** now so workers own robots later.
think: Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots is **plenty of time** for me.
By forty I'd probably be running the co-op's **design side**.
do: Buy the flat and do the **master's licence** as planned.
Push Sunwire to set up a **training fund** for members.
Set a **yearly reminder** to check how fast things are moving.
S4.quote: I'd love Sunwire to be twenty members owning a few install robots, with people like me doing the design and testing.
fieldNote: Karl is **calm** here because of savings, skills and a ten-year horizon.
He names **complacency** as the risk of a long warning.
His dream is a co-op that **owns the robots**.

steps.text: Set up a monthly member training fund at Sunwire
Finish the master electrician's licence on a normal timeline
Keep using AI daily for quotes and system design

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam's job would go first and the co-op wouldn't have time to adapt. What would help is a levy on AI companies that pays for proper retraining, and cheap loans for co-ops to buy the new machines themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the machines. I keep coming back to it because it decides everything else. If the robots belong to the people doing the work, then this is the best thing that ever happened to tradespeople.

headlineQuote: If the robots belong to the people doing the work, then this is the best thing that ever happened to tradespeople.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** electrician and part-owner of Sunwire, a twelve-person co-op fitting solar and batteries.
He uses **AI every day** for quotes and calculations and is the first to try new tools.
He lives with **Sam**, a software tester whose job is exposed to AI, and they're saving to buy.
His fear in fast pictures is for the **household**, not for his own hands-on work.
His answer to robots is **ownership**: the co-op should buy them, not compete with them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Sam's job would go first and the co-op couldn't adapt in time.
whatWouldHelp: A **levy** on AI companies to fund retraining.
**Cheap loans** for co-ops to buy robots themselves.
